original_value: AbstractRecognizing users’ daily life activities without disrupting their lifestyle is a key functionality to enable a broad variety of advanced services for a Smart City, from energy-efficient management of urban spaces to mobility optimization. In this paper, we propose a novel method for human activity recognition from a collection of outdoor mobility traces acquired through wearable devices. Our method exploits the regularities naturally present in human mobility patterns to construct syntactic models in the form of finite state automata, thanks to an approach known asgrammatical inference. We also introduce a measure ofsimilaritythat accounts for the intrinsic hierarchical nature of such models, and allows to identify the common traits in the paths induced by different activities at various granularity levels. Our method has been validated on a dataset of real traces representing movements of users in a large metropolitan area. The experimental results show the effectiveness of our similarity measure to correctly identify a set of common coarse-grained activities, as well as their refinement at a finer level of granularity.

result.paraphrase: Recognizing people’s everyday activities without disturbing their routine is an important capability for enabling many advanced Smart City services, ranging from energy-efficient urban space management to mobility optimization. In this paper, we present a new approach for human activity recognition based on a set of outdoor mobility traces collected with wearable devices. The method leverages the regular patterns inherent in human mobility to build syntactic models as finite-state automata through grammatical inference. We also propose a similarity measure that captures the intrinsic hierarchical structure of these models and makes it possible to detect shared traits in the paths generated by different activities at multiple granularity levels. We validated the method on a dataset of real traces depicting user movements in a large metropolitan area. Experimental results demonstrate that the similarity measure effectively identifies common coarse-grained activities and their finer-grained refinements.
